'''Edward Belbruno''' (born August 2, 1951) is an American mathematician. His research areas are in [[celestial mechanics]], dynamical systems, dynamical astronomy, and aerospace engineering. 

== Early life ==
Belbruno was born in the USAG Army Base in [[Heidelberg, Germany]]. He received his associate degree from [[Mitchell College]], his Bachelor of Science degree in mathematics from [[New York University]] and his PhD in mathematics from New York University's [[Courant Institute]] in 1981, where his mentor was mathematician [[Jürgen Moser]].<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
He worked as mathematician at Boston University until 1985.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=
Edward A. Belbruno|url=https://www.yu.edu/faculty/pages/belbruno-edward|access-date=10 May 2026|website=Yeshiva University|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260511054439/https://www.yu.edu/faculty/pages/belbruno-edward|archive-date=11 May 2026 }}</ref> He was employed by the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] from 1985 to 1990 as an orbital analyst on such missions as [[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo]], [[Magellan (spacecraft)|Magellan]], [[Cassini (spacecraft)|Cassini]], [[Ulysses (spacecraft)|Ulysses]], [[Mars Observer]], and others. During that time, he laid the foundations for the first systematic application of [[chaos theory]] to space flight originally called [[Interplanetary travel#Fuzzy orbits|fuzzy boundary theory]], which allows for the construction of very low energy paths for spacecraft.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 1, 2000|title=Low Energy Routes Using Chaos in Space Travel and Astronomy|url=https://ecolloq.gsfc.nasa.gov/archive/2000-Spring/announce.belbruno.html|url-status=live|website=Goddard Space Flight Center Engineering Colloquium, NASA|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010303170751/http://ecolloq.gsfc.nasa.gov:80/archive/2000-Spring/announce.belbruno.html |archive-date=2001-03-03 }}</ref>

Belbruno had first proposed using a low-energy transfer orbit for a JPL probe in 1988.  However, he faced a great deal of skepticism, and found himself in conflict with engineers.  He had also expected to make no progress on ''Hiten'', but the Japanese proved receptive to his ideas and called ballistic capture an "amazing result."  He left JPL in fall of 1990 and took a position at [[Pomona College]].<ref name="belbruno_fly">Belbruno, Edward.  ''Fly me to the moon: an insider's guide to the new science of space travel''.  Princeton University Press, 2007.</ref>

Belbruno is president and founder of the company Innovative Orbital Design, Inc., based in [[Princeton, New Jersey]] and holds patents on routes in space.  He consulted on the rescue of the [[PAS-22|Asiasat-3]] communications satellite for Hughes, although a different trajectory was ultimately used for the rescue.

Belbruno's books include ''Fly Me to the Moon'' and ''Capture Dynamics and Chaotic Motions in Celestial Mechanics''.  He is a consultant with the [[National Aeronautics and Space Administration]], and has made appearances on NBC's [[Today (NBC program)|''Today Show'']] and [[NPR]]'s ''[[Studio 360]]'' entitled "Propelled to Paint".<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 22, 2010|title=Propelled to Paint|url=https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/studio/segments/108380-propelled-to-paint|url-status=live|access-date=August 10, 2021|website=Studio 360|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210810150113/https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/studio/segments/108380-propelled-to-paint |archive-date=2021-08-10 }}</ref>

The abstract expressionist paintings of Ed Belbruno reflect both inner and outer realities. Belbruno is self-taught and draws inspiration from his subconscious and his personal life, but is also deeply influenced by his research in math, science, and astrophysics.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Artist Biography|url=https://www.edbelbruno.com/bio|url-status=live|access-date=July 28, 2021|website=Official website of Edward Belbruno|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160318144224/http://edbelbruno.com/bio/ |archive-date=2016-03-18 }}</ref> Belbruno was featured at the Shanghai Art Fair, November 2–5, 2017<ref>{{Cite web|title=Shanghai Art Fair 2017|url=https://www.agora-gallery.com/artfairs/ShanghaiArtFair2017.aspx|url-status=live|access-date=July 28, 2021|website=Agora Gallery|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171028184949/https://www.agora-gallery.com/artfairs/ShanghaiArtFair2017.aspx |archive-date=2017-10-28 }}</ref> and the West Contemporary Arts Appreciation Society exhibition, in Weihai in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|title=West Contemporary Arts Appreciation Society Exhibition|url=https://www.agora-gallery.com/artgalleryblog/agora-artists-weihai-china/|url-status=live|access-date=July 28, 2021|website=Agora Gallery|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210810144708/https://www.agora-gallery.com/artgalleryblog/agora-artists-weihai-china/ |archive-date=2021-08-10 }}</ref> An exhibition of his work at Agora Gallery (530 West 25th Street, New York) on Thursday, Nov. 14, 2019 included a screening of the documentary "Painting the Way to the Moon" and special guest [[Neil deGrasse Tyson]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dr. Edward Belbruno is Painting the Way to the Moon|url=https://blogs.yu.edu/facultynews/2019/10/09/dr-edward-belbruno-is-painting-the-way-to-the-moon/|url-status=live|access-date=July 28, 2021|website=Yeshiva University Faculty News|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805075111/https://blogs.yu.edu/facultynews/2019/10/09/dr-edward-belbruno-is-painting-the-way-to-the-moon/ |archive-date=2020-08-05 }}</ref>

A documentary by Jacob Okada called "Painting the Way to the Moon" explores the life, art, and science of NASA-JPL mathematician, Ed Belbruno, and includes a discussion on the nature of scientific creativity with Neil deGrasse Tyson. It won Best Feature Documentary at the [[Philip K. Dick]], Boston Sci-Fi, and NYLA Film Festivals.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Painting the Way to the Moon|url=https://www.firstencounterproductions.com/paintingthewaytothemoon|url-status=live|access-date=January 28, 2020|website=First Encounter Productions|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210810143435/https://www.firstencounterproductions.com/paintingthewaytothemoon |archive-date=2021-08-10 }}</ref>

Belbruno was awarded the [[Humboldt Prize|Humboldt Research Award]] in November, 2017 in recognition for his “Accomplishments in Research and Teaching in Mathematics as Applied to Celestial Mechanics, Astrodynamics and AstroPhysics”.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Edward Belbruno Humboldt Foundation Profile|url=https://www.humboldt-foundation.de/en/connect/explore-the-humboldt-network/singleview?tx_rsmavhsolr_solrview%5BpPersonId%5D=1193397&cHash=5c96c830b782ec2bf954a24f6db0c71c|url-status=live|access-date=July 28, 2021|website=Alexander von Humboldt Foundation|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210729070457/https://www.humboldt-foundation.de/en/connect/explore-the-humboldt-network/singleview?tx_rsmavhsolr_solrview%5BpPersonId%5D=1193397&cHash=5c96c830b782ec2bf954a24f6db0c71c |archive-date=2021-07-29 }}</ref> The Humboldt Research Award is Germany's most prestigious award in mathematics and sciences which supported Belbruno in a yearlong stay in Germany at the University of Ausburg.<ref>{{Cite web|date=Nov 30, 2017|title=Astrophysics’ Ed Belbruno wins Humboldt Research Award|url=https://web.astro.princeton.edu/news/astrophysics’-ed-belbruno-wins-humboldt-research-award|url-status=live|website=Princeton University Department of Astrophysical Sciences|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171215223809/https://web.astro.princeton.edu/news/astrophysics%E2%80%99-ed-belbruno-wins-humboldt-research-award |archive-date=2017-12-15 }}</ref>

Currently, Belbruno is a Clinical Professor of Mathematics at [[Yeshiva University]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Yeshiva University Faculty Directory|url=https://www.yu.edu/faculty/pages/belbruno-edward|url-status=live|access-date=June 19, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200812155845/https://www.yu.edu/faculty/pages/belbruno-edward |archive-date=2020-08-12 }}</ref> and a Visiting Research Collaborator at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Princeton University Department of Astrophysical Sciences Faculty Directory|url=https://web.astro.princeton.edu/people/edward-belbruno|url-status=live|access-date=June 19, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201217202612/https://web.astro.princeton.edu/people/edward-belbruno |archive-date=2020-12-17 }}</ref>
